1366.title: Days for everyone
1366.hook: Eid is for the poor, the orphan, the traveler too
1366.howItsDone: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, Muslims pay zakat al-fitr so that people in need can eat on the feast day, and at Eid al-Adha the meat of the sacrifice is shared with the poor; mosques and families often open their Eid meals to people who are alone, far from home or in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eid al-Adha: first the prayer, then the sacrifice, then the meat carried out the door.

Al-Bukhari keeps a sharp little saying, reported from Abu Hurayrah. In paraphrase: the worst food is the food of a wedding feast where the rich are invited and the poor are left out. Not spoiled food, not stolen food. A good meal, at a happy party, with the wrong guest list. The saying is about a wedding. Some readers hear it about any feast, the two Eids included. So, at the end of the festival year, a question about the guest list: who is Eid for?
screen: `THE WORST FOOD.` → `THE WRONG GUEST LIST.` → `WHO IS EID FOR?`

segments.voice: Look at how the two Eids are built, and the guest list is written into them. Before Eid al-Fitr comes zakat al-fitr, the charity of the fast's end. Ibn 'Abbas reports in Sunan Abi Dawud that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, made it a purification for the one who fasted and food for the poor, and that it counts as zakat when paid before the prayer. Some read that timing as a way to make sure the poor eat on the feast day too. At Eid al-Adha, as yesterday, the meat leaves the house by design. Then the orphan. Surah al-Insan praises people who, in Pickthall's words, "feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him." A day of new clothes is a hard day for a child with no one to buy them, and some communities make a point of new clothes and gifts for orphans before Eid. Then the traveler. The Qur'an names the wayfarer, the person far from home, among those owed kindness: on a feast day, the student who couldn't fly home, the new arrival, the night-shift worker. And now the whole year we've walked: the sacred months, Muharram and Ashura, Rabi' al-Awwal, Rajab and Sha'ban, Ramadan from planning to the last ten, both Eids, Dhul Qa'dah's packing, Dhul Hijjah at home. Each one, at its best, with room at the table.
screen: `FOOD FOR THE POOR BEFORE THE PRAYER.` · `THE ORPHAN AT THE FEAST.` · `THE TRAVELER FAR FROM HOME.` · `A YEAR OF DAYS, ROOM AT THE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Go slowly through the people you know, at work, on your street, in your family, and look for the one likely to spend the next holiday alone: a widowed neighbor, a colleague far from home, a student. Let one face come, and picture the invitation, a meal, a coffee, a walk. If you pray, remember them by name; if not, hold the picture of the empty chair filled.
Days for everyone. The festival year built so that the poor eat, the orphan is dressed and the traveler is fed on the feast day too. Today's word.
Your line: no one alone on eid. The table was always meant to have room. Next, a new stretch: many ways of being Muslim.

1367.title: Many ways of being Muslim
1367.hook: one faith lived in many languages, customs and schools
1367.howItsDone: Muslims in many countries share the shahadah, the daily prayers in Arabic and the qibla toward Makkah, while following different schools of law and keeping the customs, languages and foods of their own places.

segments.voice: Yesterday, days for everyone: the poor fed before the prayer, the orphan and the traveler at the table.

One row at Friday prayer in a big city mosque, shoulder to shoulder. A taxi driver who grew up speaking Somali. A student from Indonesia. A grandfather from Lahore in a crisp white shalwar kameez. A convert who learned the prayer not long ago and still watches the person beside him for the next move. After the prayer they'll go home to different kitchens and different languages. But right now the imam says Allahu akbar, al-Fatiha is recited in Arabic, and the whole row faces the same direction.
screen: `ONE ROW, MANY HOMES.` → `THE SAME FATIHA.` → `THE SAME DIRECTION.`

segments.voice: Start with Surah al-Hujurat, in Pickthall's translation: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Nations and tribes aren't a problem to be solved; they're there so people can know each other. The verse goes straight on: "Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct." Surah al-Rum lists the creation of the heavens and the earth, and in the same breath, "the difference of your languages and colours." A world of accents, on purpose. Then schools. Among Sunni Muslims there are the schools of law named for their teachers: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali. Among Shia Muslims, the Ja'fari school, and there are Ibadi Muslims as well. In some mosques people stand with hands folded, in others with arms at their sides. Each follows a school with its own scholars and reasons. Then customs. What's cooked for Eid, what's worn to Friday prayer, how a wedding goes: these grow from places, not only from texts. Through all of it, the center holds: the shahadah, the prayer in Arabic, the same qibla. Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying, in paraphrase, that Allah doesn't look at your outward forms or your wealth, but at your hearts and your deeds.
screen: `NATIONS AND TRIBES, TO KNOW EACH OTHER.` · `LANGUAGES AMONG HIS SIGNS.` · `SCHOOLS: ONE PRAYER, SEVERAL WAYS.` · `CUSTOMS GROW FROM PLACES.`

segments.voice: Think of a place you've never connected with Islam: Senegal, Bosnia, China, Trinidad, the Philippines. Pick one and wonder, without needing answers, what Friday would look like there, and what Eid would smell like. If you pray, remember the people of that place.
Many ways of being Muslim. One faith, kept in many languages, customs and schools of law, with the same prayer at its center. Today's word.
screen: `MANY WAYS OF BEING MUSLIM — today's word`.

1368.title: The mosque community
1368.howItsDone: Mosques are often run by volunteer boards and committees alongside an imam, and host weekend schools for children, iftars in Ramadan, funeral services, food drives and open days, with members volunteering for cleaning, teaching, cooking and parking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many ways of being Muslim: one row, many homes, the same Fatiha.

Ask who runs a mosque, and the quick answer is the imam. Then look on a Saturday morning at a mosque in the suburbs. In the basement, kids at folding tables learn the Arabic letters, and one is drawing a dinosaur in the margin. Upstairs, the committee argues politely about whether the new carpet should be green or blue. In the kitchen, two aunties plan next month's iftar. Out front, a man in a reflective vest sorts out the parking. Nobody here is praying right now. And all of it is the mosque.
screen: `A WEEKEND SCHOOL IN THE BASEMENT.` → `A COMMITTEE AND A CARPET.` → `ALL OF IT IS THE MOSQUE.`

segments.voice: Begin with a surprise from al-Bukhari. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, listed things given to him, and one was this, in paraphrase: the earth has been made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification, so wherever the time of prayer reaches you, pray. Any clean patch of ground will do. Then why build one? Look at the Prophet's mosque in Madinah. Al-Bukhari reports that when it was built, the Prophet carried building materials alongside his companions. Before there was a committee or a carpet, there were people hauling things together. Then the person nobody noticed. Al-Bukhari tells of someone who used to sweep the mosque; the narrator isn't sure whether it was a man or a woman. When the sweeper died, people didn't think to tell the Prophet. Later he asked about the sweeper and heard. He said, in paraphrase: why didn't you tell me? Show me the grave. And he went and prayed there. The sweeper was missed by name. Today, a mosque is often a prayer hall plus everything around it: an imam who leads and teaches, a board that pays the bills, volunteers for the weekend school, the funeral committee, the iftar kitchen, the food pantry. The prayer could happen anywhere. What the building gathers is people, and people are how a stranger in town finds a meal, a funeral prayer, a teacher for their kid.
screen: `THE EARTH IS A PLACE OF PRAYER.` · `THE PROPHET CARRIED LOADS TOO.` · `THE SWEEPER WAS MISSED.` · `A HALL AND EVERYONE AROUND IT.`

segments.voice: Picture the scene again, the basement school, the kitchen, the parking vest, the broom, and ask which job you could do: reading to kids, stacking chairs, washing up after an iftar, driving someone older to Friday prayer. If you're not Muslim, some mosques welcome help with open days, food drives and interfaith meals. Let one small job come clear, and if you pray, ask that it be accepted.
The mosque community. The people around the prayer hall: imam, board, teachers, cooks, sweepers, volunteers. The building gathers them; they make it a mosque. Today's word.
Your line: the mosque is people. Any clean ground holds a prayer; people make a mosque. Until tomorrow.

1369.title: The imam's role
1369.hook: the imam leads prayer and teaches, with no priesthood between a person and Allah
1369.howItsDone: An imam leads the congregational prayer and, at a mosque, often preaches the Friday sermon, teaches and counsels; any qualified Muslim may lead a prayer, and individual prayer and supplication are made directly to Allah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mosque community: a basement school, a committee, a sweeper missed by name.

Three friends on a road trip stop at a rest area when the time for prayer comes in. No mosque. No imam. One of them lays a jacket on the grass to mark the direction. Then a small, friendly argument: you lead. No, you lead, you know more Qur'an. Finally one steps a pace forward, the other two line up behind, and the prayer begins. For those few minutes, he's the imam. Then the prayer ends, and he's just the guy driving the next leg.
screen: `A REST AREA, A JACKET ON THE GRASS.` → `YOU LEAD. NO, YOU LEAD.` → `FOR A FEW MINUTES, THE IMAM.`

segments.voice: In Sahih Muslim, Abu Mas'ud reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying, in paraphrase: the one who leads the people should be the one who best recites the Book of Allah, and if they're equal in that, the one who knows the Sunnah best. That's the qualification. Not a family line, not an ordination. Recitation and knowledge. So at a rest area, any qualified Muslim can lead. At a mosque, the full-time imam usually leads the daily prayers, often gives the Friday sermon, teaches, marries couples, sits with grieving families and answers questions: a teacher, and a pastor of sorts in the everyday sense. Now what the imam doesn't do. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh. I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me." Allah answers the one who calls, directly. The imam stands in front so the rows can pray together. He doesn't carry their prayers for them, and no one needs him present to pray. Another verse puts it closer still: "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." Last, a word with more than one size. The Qur'an uses it for Ibrahim: "Lo! I have appointed thee a leader for mankind." The Arabic there is imam. And Shia Muslims use Imam, with a capital I, for the Imams of the Prophet's family, a role far larger than leading a prayer. Same word, different weight.
screen: `THE BEST RECITER LEADS.` · `TEACHER, PREACHER, NEIGHBOR.` · `I AM NIGH: NO ONE IN BETWEEN.` · `ONE WORD, DIFFERENT WEIGHTS.`

segments.voice: Set aside any waiting for the right person, the right building or the right words, and bring to mind one thing on your heart today: a worry, a thank-you, a question. If you pray, say it to Allah in your own words, silently, with no one in between; if not, put it into one plain sentence and let it sit there, unhurried.
The imam's role. To lead the prayer, teach and serve, chosen for recitation and knowledge, standing in front of the rows, not between a person and Allah. Today's word.
Your line: no one in between. The one in front leads the rows; the prayer is still yours. Go gently.

1370.title: The Deobandi and Barelvi traditions
1370.hook: two South Asian Sunni movements from the nineteenth century, differing on devotions to saints and the Prophet ﷺ
1370.howItsDone: Deobandi and Barelvi Muslims are Sunni Muslims of the Hanafi school with roots in South Asia and communities around the world; Barelvi communities often celebrate the Mawlid and honor saints' shrines, while Deobandi communities emphasize close following of the Sunnah and madrasa study and are cautious about some of those practices.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the imam's role: the best reciter steps forward, and no one stands between a person and Allah.

Two mosques on the same street, in a city in Pakistan, or Bradford, or Chicago. Both Sunni. Both follow the Hanafi school of law. Both pray the same prayers at the same times. At one, when Friday prayer ends, the whole room rises and sends greetings to the Prophet in Urdu poetry, together, standing. At the other, people file out quietly, and a teacher stays behind for a class on following his Sunnah closely, which is how that teacher says he is best honored. Same street, same school. Different ways of showing honor.
screen: `TWO MOSQUES, ONE STREET.` → `SAME SCHOOL, SAME PRAYERS.` → `DIFFERENT WAYS OF SHOWING HONOR.`

segments.voice: Both names come from places in north India. Deobandi is named for Deoband, a town where a religious school, the Darul Uloom, was founded by scholars including Muhammad Qasim Nanautawi and Rashid Ahmad Gangohi. Barelvi is named for Bareilly, the hometown of the scholar Ahmad Raza Khan. Barelvi Muslims often prefer to call themselves Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah, the people of the Sunnah and the community. What they share: both are Sunni, both Hanafi, both have Sufi teachers and lineages in their history, and both hold the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at the center. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." Neither disputes that. Where they differ is how. Barelvi Muslims, in their own words, express love for the Prophet openly: the Mawlid, his birthday, with gatherings, poetry and standing to greet him, and honoring the saints at their shrines. Ahmad Raza Khan himself wrote devotional poetry in the Prophet's praise. Deobandi Muslims, in their own words, put the weight on following the Sunnah closely, are cautious about practices they see as later additions, including some of these, and built a network of madrasas focused on study. The disagreements are real, and sometimes sharp. But the two mosques share a school, a creed and a Prophet, and one line of the Qur'an hangs over both doors: "And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate."

1371.title: The Tablighi Jamaat
1371.hook: a worldwide movement of traveling preachers calling Muslims back to prayer
1371.howItsDone: Members of the Tablighi Jamaat volunteer to travel at their own expense in small groups, stay in mosques, go door to door inviting Muslims to the congregational prayer, and hold readings from collections of virtues and hadith; the movement describes itself as non-political.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Deobandi and Barelvi traditions: two mosques on one street, the same school, different ways of showing honor. Today, a movement from that same world.

Late afternoon, a doorbell rings. On the step are a few men you've never seen: one older, one barely out of college, one with a duffel bag over his shoulder. They're not selling anything. They're not collecting money. They've come from another city, and they're sleeping on the floor of the local mosque this week. One smiles: we're just reminding our brothers about the prayer. Maghrib is at the mosque tonight, with a short talk after. Will you come? Then they thank you and walk on to the next door.

segments.voice: Tabligh means conveying, passing the message on. Jamaat means a group. The movement began in Mewat, near Delhi, with a Deobandi scholar named Muhammad Ilyas Kandhlawi, who wanted ordinary Muslims, not only scholars, to carry the basics of faith and prayer to each other. Members volunteer to go out, in their own words, in the path of Allah, for a set stretch of time, in small groups. They pay their own way, carry their own bedding, stay in mosques, cook and eat together, and take turns serving each other. In the afternoons they walk the streets around the mosque, knocking on Muslim doors, inviting people back to the congregation. In the evenings they read together from collections of virtues and hadith. The ground it stands on: the Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation, "And there may spring from you a nation who invite to goodness, and enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency." And al-Bukhari reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying, in paraphrase: convey from me, even if it's a single verse. Tabligh is that conveying, done on foot. The movement describes itself as staying out of politics and out of arguments between schools, and as speaking mainly to Muslims, not seeking converts. It has admirers and critics among Muslims. Some praise how it brings people back to the prayer. Some scholars question parts of its reading books, or long absences from home, and members answer those questions in their own terms.
screen: `TABLIGH: PASSING IT ON.` · `OUT IN SMALL GROUPS, ON FOOT.` · `CONVEY FROM ME, EVEN ONE VERSE.` · `NO POLITICS, MAINLY TO MUSLIMS.`

segments.voice: Picture yourself with the duffel bag: a floor to sleep on, someone else's cooking, a street you don't know, a door you have to knock on. Notice what comes up, nerves, curiosity, embarrassment, and then picture the other side of the door: someone who hasn't been to the mosque in years, hearing their name said kindly. If you pray, remember the people who knock and the people who answer.
The Tablighi Jamaat. A movement of volunteers who travel in small groups, stay in mosques and knock on doors, calling Muslims back to the prayer. Today's word.

1372.title: The Salafi approach
1372.hook: a movement to follow the early generations closely and avoid later additions, itself diverse
1372.howItsDone: Salafi Muslims describe their approach as following the Qur'an and the Sunnah as the companions and the generations after them understood them, studying the texts directly and avoiding devotions they regard as later additions; they differ among themselves on method and on public life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Tablighi Jamaat: small groups on foot, knocking on doors, calling Muslims back to the prayer.

A chain of people, hand to hand. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says something. A companion hears it and passes it on. Someone who learned from that companion passes it on again. Al-Bukhari keeps a saying about those first links. In paraphrase: the best people are my generation, then those who come after them, then those who come after them. Some Muslims draw a plain conclusion: if the first links were the best, the surest way to practice Islam is to stand as close to them as you can. That's where today's movement starts, in its own words.
screen: `A CHAIN, HAND TO HAND.` → `MY GENERATION, THEN THE NEXT.` → `STAND CLOSE TO THE FIRST.`

segments.voice: First, the name, as Salafis explain it. They take it from a phrase, al-salaf al-salih, which they render as the righteous predecessors: the companions and the generations who learned from them. A Salafi, in their own description, follows the Qur'an and the Sunnah as those early generations understood them. Second, what they avoid. Salafi teachers point to a hadith in al-Bukhari and Muslim. In paraphrase: whoever brings into this matter of ours something that is not part of it, it is rejected. So they are wary of practices they see as later additions, and ask of any devotion: did the Prophet and his companions do this? Tawhid, Allah's oneness, sits at the center of how they teach. Third, the movement is itself diverse. There is no single Salafi headquarters. Some teachers focus on study and personal practice and stay out of public life; others take part in it. Salafis argue with each other about method, about politics, about how strict to be with someone who disagrees. Lumping them together misses those arguments. Fourth, the conversation around them. Muslims who are not Salafi also love the first generations, and say so. Scholars of the traditional schools hold that the schools and the long line of later scholarship are how a Muslim reaches those generations faithfully, not a step away from them. Salafis answer that the texts should be read directly, with the early generations as the guide. Each side says it is following the companions. They differ about the road back.
screen: `AL-SALAF AL-SALIH: THE PREDECESSORS.` · `IS IT SOMETHING NEW? THEN IT'S REJECTED.` · `ITSELF DIVERSE, AND ARGUING.` · `EACH SIDE SAYS: THE COMPANIONS.`

segments.voice: Let each breath be one link in the chain from the hook: the Prophet, a companion, the one who learned from that companion.
